DOCUMENT:
Menu Pricing Review: Spring 2026
The Copper Kettle, prepared by the General Manager for the owners, March 2026

1. Purpose
This paper reviews main-course pricing and menu mix and proposes changes to take effect with the spring menu on 1 April 2026. Our overall gross margin on food, across all courses, has slipped from 70% to 67% over the past year as ingredient costs have risen faster than our prices, and we last changed main-course prices in September 2024.

2. Trading pattern
The Copper Kettle is a 64-cover restaurant open for lunch and dinner from Wednesday to Sunday. We serve an average of 1,050 main courses a week, with Friday and Saturday dinner accounting for just under half. Our customers are mainly local, with a strong repeat base: our booking system shows that around 60% of bookings come from guests who have dined with us in the past six months.

Table 1. Main courses, average weekly sales (January-February 2026)
Dish | Menu price | Food cost per plate | Gross margin | Plates per week
Fish and chips | £16.50 | £5.10 | 69% | 310
Beef burger | £15.00 | £4.20 | 72% | 260
Chicken curry | £14.50 | £3.60 | 75% | 180
Sirloin steak | £26.00 | £10.40 | 60% | 120
Mushroom risotto | £14.00 | £2.80 | 80% | 90
Other mains (specials) | various | various | 64% | 90

3. Competitor prices
We checked menus at the five restaurants we regard as our closest competitors. Their fish and chips ranges from £16.95 to £19.00, burgers from £15.50 to £17.50 and sirloin steak from £27.00 to £32.00. Our prices for these three dishes are the lowest in the group.

4. Supplier costs
Our meat supplier has given notice that beef prices will rise by 12% from 1 April 2026, reflecting national cattle prices. Other supplier prices are expected to be broadly stable over the spring. Fish prices have been volatile but are currently close to their 2025 average.

5. Proposals
5.1 Price increases. Raise fish and chips to £17.50, the beef burger to £16.00 and the sirloin steak to £28.00. All three would remain below the midpoint of the competitor range for that dish.

5.2 Remove the mushroom risotto. Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place. We propose replacing it with a seasonal vegetarian special at the same price.

5.3 Projected effect. If volumes hold, the price increases add £1.00 per plate on 310 fish and chips, £1.00 on 260 burgers and £2.00 on 120 steaks, a total of £810 a week in additional gross profit, or £42,120 a year. Because our prices remain competitive and our customer base is loyal, we expect volumes to hold. The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target.

6. Communication
Menus will be reprinted for 1 April. Staff will be briefed on the changes, and we will not draw attention to the increases on the menu. We will monitor plates sold per dish weekly for the first eight weeks against the January to February baseline.

7. Risks
Some regular guests may notice the increases. However, the last price change in 2024 had no visible effect on bookings, and the new prices remain competitive. Weekday lunch trade is more price-sensitive than dinner, but it represents a small share of main-course sales.

8. Recommendation
We recommend that the owners approve the three price increases and the replacement of the mushroom risotto from 1 April 2026. Together these changes add about £42,000 a year in gross profit, improve our margin and keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [misread_evidence] at: "Risotto has the weakest margin on the menu and the lowest sales, so it is not earning its place." -- Table 1 shows mushroom risotto has the highest gross margin on the menu (80%); the weakest is sirloin steak (60%). Lowest sales is correct (90 plates, tied with specials), but the margin claim misreads the table.
2. [missing_consideration] at: "The increases would lift main-course gross margin to about 71%, helping restore our 70% overall target." -- The projection uses current food costs, but section 4 states beef prices rise 12% from 1 April, the same date as the new prices. Burgers and steaks (380 plates a week) would see higher food costs (e.g. about £1.25 more per steak), eroding much of the projected gain; the margin and profit projections never account for it.
3. [inconsistency] at: "keep us competitively priced, across our six trading days a week" -- Section 2 says the restaurant is open Wednesday to Sunday, i.e. five days a week; the recommendation refers to six trading days.

REVIEW:
The review is clearly written, and most of its arithmetic is correct. But two of its central claims don't survive a check against its own tables:

- **The risotto has the highest margin on the menu, not the weakest.**
- **The £810/week projection ignores the 12% beef rise reported in section 4.** That rise absorbs a large part of the gain on the burger and steak.

## What checks out

- **Table 1 margins are computed correctly.** For example, fish is (16.50 − 5.10) / 16.50 = 69%. The plate counts sum to 1,050.
- **All three new prices are below the competitor midpoints.** The midpoints are £17.98 for fish, £16.50 for burgers and £29.50 for steak.
- **The £810 sum is right:** 310 × £1 + 260 × £1 + 120 × £2 = £810/week, or £42,120/year.
- **"About 71%" is roughly right on the paper's own assumptions:** volumes hold and costs don't change.

## Major issues

**1. The risotto claim is the reverse of the data.**
Risotto has an **80%** margin, the highest on the menu. It also earns £11.20 gross profit per plate, more than the burger (£10.80) or curry (£10.90). Its 90 plates a week tie with specials for lowest volume. They are not uniquely lowest.

Replacing it could also cost money. If the new special performs like the current specials (64% margin at the same £14 price), gross profit falls from £11.20 to about £8.96 a plate. On 90 plates that is about **£200 a week lost**, which the projection doesn't include.

There's also a question the data can't answer: is the risotto the only vegetarian main? If so, it may bring in whole tables, not just one plate. A seasonal special may still be a good idea, but the case for it has to rest on something other than margin.

**2. The beef rise is reported, then left out.**
From 1 April, a 12% beef rise adds up to:
- **£0.50 per burger** (£4.20 → £4.70)
- **£1.25 per steak** (£10.40 → £11.65)

These are upper bounds, since not all of each plate's cost is beef. On current volumes that is up to **about £280 a week**. Netting it off:

| | Weekly | Annual |
|---|---|---|
| Paper's projection | £810 | £42,120 |
| Less beef rise (upper bound) | −£281 | −£14,600 |
| Less risotto replacement, if special performs like current specials | −£200 | −£10,500 |
| **Net, on these assumptions** | **≈ £330** | **≈ £17,000** |

Most of the beef cost falls on the steak and burger, so the true figure probably lies between about £330 and £600 a week, not £810. With the beef rise included, **steak margin falls even after the £2 increase**, from 60% to about 58%. The burger falls from 72% to about 71%. Main-course margin stays roughly where it is now (~69–70%), rather than rising to 71%.

**3. Check whether margins are calculated on VAT-inclusive prices.**
UK menu prices include 20% VAT. If Table 1's margins use menu prices, every margin is overstated and every £1 price rise brings in only about £0.83. On that basis the £810 becomes about £675 before the other adjustments. If the margins are already net of VAT, ignore this point, but the paper should say which basis it uses.

## Other issues

- **"We remain the value option" overstates the position.** The paper currently says we are cheapest in the group on all three dishes. After the change we would be cheapest on none of them: each new price is above the lowest competitor price (£16.95, £15.50, £27.00). "Below the midpoint" is accurate. "Cheapest" no longer would be.
- **"Volumes will hold" is assumed, not shown.** A regular base cuts both ways, because regular guests are the ones who know the old prices. A useful figure for the owners is the break-even volume loss: the price rises pay for themselves unless volumes fall by more than about **8–9% on fish and burgers, and 12% on steak**, compared with not raising prices.
- **The evidence about the 2024 price change is thin.** "No visible effect on bookings" measures bookings, not dishes chosen or spend per head, and it wasn't measured formally.
- **Weekday lunch is called "small" without a figure.** Friday and Saturday dinner are just under half of covers, so lunches and the other dinners make up the rest. The lunch share should be stated.
- **Monitoring against the January–February baseline will mislead.** April and May trade differently from winter, and Easter falls on 5 April 2026. Compare against the same weeks of 2025 instead.
- **Trading days are inconsistent.** Section 2 says Wednesday to Sunday (five days), while section 8 says "six trading days."
- **The data period is short and seasonal.** Two winter months may understate spring demand for lighter dishes, including the risotto.

## On the author's description

Several claims in the description don't match the paper:

- **"Latest supplier information" is not used.** The beef rise is reported but missing from the projection.
- **"Weakest margin" is wrong.** It is the strongest margin on the menu.
- **"Full competitor price check" covers three dishes only.** Curry and risotto were not checked.
- **"Simple to check" is true, and checking is what exposes the gaps.**
- **"Low-risk" is not quantified.** The break-even volume figures above would let the owners judge it.

## Suggested revisions

1. Keep the three price increases. They are reasonable and still sit below competitor midpoints. Restate the projection net of the beef rise, and state the VAT basis used.
2. Withdraw the margin case for removing the risotto. If the menu change is still wanted, argue it on other grounds and cost the replacement special.
3. Add the break-even volume figures and lunch's share of trade.
4. Monitor against the same weeks of 2025, and track spend per head as well as plates sold.

With those changes, the paper would show a modest, defensible improvement of perhaps £17,000–£30,000 a year, instead of the £42,000 currently claimed.
